blurb: Calling a function value whose type returns `Effect[T]` is an effect, just as calling a capability is, and effects are only allowed in a body that is itself effectful, one whose return type is an `Effect`. Bynk makes effects explicit so that a function's signature tells you whether it can touch the outside world: a function that returns a plain `Int` is pure and can be reasoned about as such. A call through a parameter would hide an effect behind that signature, so it is refused. Either make the function return `Effect[T]` and bind the call with `<-`, or take a pure function instead. A capability call from a handler that has not declared it is a different mistake, `bynk.given.undeclared_capability`.
summary: An effectful function value was called in a pure context; like a capability call, it is legal only where the enclosing body is effectful.
